newsitem.title: CROATIA: Audi, BMW, Mercedes outselling Ladas in Croatia.
newsitem.headline: Audi, BMW, Mercedes outselling Ladas in Croatia.

text.p: Former communist Europe is notorious for clunky Trabants and Ladas cluttering the streets and polluting the air, but Croatian car buyers prefer Audis, BMWs and Mercedes-Benz.

Croatia, once part of Yugoslavia, was unique in the region last year with each German luxury automaker outselling all communist-era brands on its market -- at least according to the quasi-official data available at Zagreb's sixth annual motor show, which opened on April 7 and runs to April 13.
New car sales in Croatia last year included 843 Audis, 536 Mercedes and 367 BMWs, and many more used versions.

Meanwhile, only 354 new Russia-made Ladas, the sole brand on offer from the old East bloc, were bought. Serbian automaker Zastava, once popular in Croatia, no longer sells here after four years of war between Croats and Serbs.
"Croatia consumers are accustomed to good cars," said Neven Dunkic, sales manager Audi at Auto Centar Zubak Zagrebacka BB, the importer for German automaker Volkswagen AG.
"Before fighting began in 1991, Croatia enjoyed living standards three-to-five times higher than other countries in eastern Europe," Dunkic said.

Indeed, the former Yugoslavia, which broke early from the Soviet-controlled trading alliance COMECON, was the region's only country during the Cold War regularly to build and import modern cars from western Europe.
Former Yugoslavia had been home to automotive ventures with Fiat SPA, General Motors Corp unit Adam Opel AG, Mercedes-Benz, PSA Peugeot Citroen, and Renault SA as well as Audi and VW.
"Now that the fighting has stopped, we expect a lot of investors and tourists to return, which will help us recover our previous lifestyle," Dunkic said.

"But 15 to 20 percent of the population already can afford Audis. Owners of boutiques, restaurants and other small businesses -- they are young, and they are buying Audis because our cars have a young image."
However, car salesmen privately admitted that many people earned the money for expensive cars during the war by selling contraband, especially weapons.

BMW is the most popular luxury brand in Croatia, counting all cars new and used. The estimated 600,000 cars on the roads include roughly 40,000 BMWs, 16,000 Audis and 11,000 Mercedes, according to the official importers of these brands.

"Croatia has sold more BMWs than any other country in eastern Europe in this year's first quarter, except possibly the Czech Republic,"said Miroslav Grgic, managing director of Tomic and Co DOO, BMW's importer in Croatia.

Grgic acknowledged BMW was popular partly because Tomic offered cash-strapped Croatians options to buy BMWs on credit with no downpayment, provided their monthly income was double their monthly loan repayments.
Unlike BMW, Mercedes-Benz has sold no cars on loans.

"All of our passenger cars are sold for cash," said Eugen Sinicic, a salesman for Euroline DD, the Croatian importer for Mercedes-Benz. "Everything is paid before the car is delivered. There are no possibilities for credit."
But not all BMWs sold in Croatia are new, Grgic said. Consumers bought the rest probably not on the black market, but the grey market, he added.
The most common origin of used BMWs has been nearby Italy, and the most popular model has been five-series turbo diesels.

"In recent years, the Italian lira has weakened, and the German mark has strengthened," Grgic said. "That made cars cheap in Italy, and Croatians have been able to go there and come back with BMWs. The diesel cars have been popular mainly because diesel fuel is cheaper than petrol."
And not all BMWs sold in Croatia stay in Croatia, Grgic said. No exact statistics are published, but people in Croat-controlled Bosnia can visit Croatia to buy cars and then return home, he said.

"These cars are considered to be re-exports from Croatia, so no duties or taxes are paid on them," he said, noting that levies on BMWs can be as high as 45 percent. "I know some Bosnians who bought cars in Croatia and went back with them."
-- Zagreb newsroom (385 1) 455 7075
